endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Document rules for truncation and summarization when clinical records exceed context window limits — truncation decisions affect what information the model acts on.

evidence.title: Summarize-then-Prompt: A Novel Prompt Engineering Strategy for Generating High-Quality Discharge Summaries
evidence.outcome: Completeness and correctness of hospital course summaries
evidence.quote: The summarize-then-prompt strategy outperformed direct concatenation strategy in both completeness (4.28 ± 0.63 vs. 4.01 ± 0.69, p < 0.001) and correctness (4.37 ± 0.54 vs. 4.17 ± 0.57, p = 0.002) of the summarization of the hospital course.

evidence.title: EHR-MCP: Real-world Evaluation of Clinical Information Retrieval by Large Language Models via Model Context Protocol
evidence.outcome: Risk of long EHR tool responses exceeding the LLM context window
evidence.effect: EHR-MCP responses were reliable, but long and repetitive data risked exceeding the context window; no numbers reported.
evidence.quote: Responses from EHR-MCP were reliable, though long and repetitive data risked exceeding the context window.

evidence.title: Revenue-sensitive evaluation of AI-assisted ICD-10-CM coding and human-AI collaboration under dual DRG payment systems
evidence.effect: BioClinicalBERT F1-micro 0.4645 vs TF-IDF 0.5528; 99.7% exceeded 512 tokens.
evidence.quote: The self-trained TF-IDF baseline achieved F1-micro of 0.5528 on the restricted top-50 label space, while BioClinicalBERT reached only 0.4645, underperforming the simpler baseline because its 512-token limit discards most of each discharge summary (99.7% exceeded this length).

evidence.title: Will My Assistant Remember My Allergy? What Personal LLM Assistants Forget When Conversation Memory Is Compressed
evidence.outcome: Loss of safety-critical facts when conversation memory is compressed or truncated
evidence.effect: Training-free eviction policies fail to rank the allergy fact highly enough; allergy survives 0-1% of the time versus 97% with full memory, and the budget needed to keep it is too large to be worth compressing.
evidence.quote: Hide the question until after compression and the advantage vanishes: on PA-Bench, 100 assistant conversations we construct, an allergy mentioned in passing survives to the question that needs it 0--1% of the time, against 97% with full memory.

evidence.title: FHIRBench: Benchmarking FHIR Clinical Data Serialization Strategies for Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Inference failure on long, complex patient records within nominal context window
evidence.effect: Llama 3.1 70B showed 100% inference failure on complex patients despite operating within its nominal context window.
evidence.quote: Fourth, Llama 3.1 70B exhibits 100% inference failure on complex patients despite operating within its nominal context window, revealing a patient-safety gap where AI assistance fails precisely for the patients who need it most.

commentary.bottom_line: One offline study of 50 hospital stays found that a summarization approach produced hospital course summaries rated more complete and correct, but no study tested whether documenting truncation or reconciliation rules changes model outputs or patient outcomes. Four hazard studies show that long or truncated records can drop facts or cause model failure, which supports the concern but does not show that the practice resolves it.

perspectives.view: The single test is a retrospective rater study of 50 stays. It reports completeness of 4.28 vs 4.01 and correctness of 4.37 vs 4.17. It evaluates a summarization method rather than the act of documenting rules, and no study addresses reconciling conflicting EHR values. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In a benchmark of 100 conversations, an allergy fact survived memory compression 0 to 1% of the time, compared with 97% with full memory. This suggests truncation can silently remove safety facts. Written rules may help reviewers see what a model never received, but no study shows that documentation catches such omissions before they reach patients.

In the MIMIC-IV study, 99.7% of admissions exceeded 512 tokens, and truncated BioClinicalBERT scored F1-micro 0.4645 against 0.5528 for TF-IDF. Llama 3.1 70B failed on all complex synthetic FHIR records within its nominal window, and an 8-patient EHR tool study found long, repetitive responses risked exceeding it. Rules may need to address complexity as well as length.

The only endorsement comes from the CHAI governance playbooks, which list documentation of truncation and summarization rules as a must. The supplied sources contain no federal or state requirement on input truncation or on reconciling conflicting EHR values. The practice therefore rests on voluntary governance guidance.

No study reports the payer mix, language, or literacy of included patients, and the one test did not report its setting. The largest hazard dataset uses MIMIC-IV admissions with a Taiwan DRG approximation. Whether truncation or reconciliation rules perform differently for Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients has not been tested.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares model outputs or clinical outcomes with and without documented truncation, summarization, or reconciliation rules, and none tests methods for resolving conflicting EHR values. The burden of maintaining such rules is also unmeasured. A prospective evaluation in live workflows that measures omitted safety facts, such as allergies, and whether reviewers detect those omissions would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the tests or hazard studies reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients cannot assume that the reported gains in the completeness and correctness of summaries apply to their records.
